Here are four updates from past letter-writers.
h
1. I’m supposed to share a special project I’m working on during quarantine — and I don’t have one (#5 at the link)
q
I’m so grateful you answered so quickly. I woke up to your response the morning I had to share my pandemic hobby.
q

For context, I was on a team leading crisis communications for a healthcare operation serving 9.2 million patients worldwide. Everything was changing, and we had to cut and redo products before they left draft because the information kept changing.
q

We had our meeting, and it was my turn to share. I decided to be honest. I said that the nature of our work and having to do all the outside stuff for my household because of my partner’s health condition was wearing me out. I was tired and scared. My only goal each day was to make it to bedtime so I could get up and do it all over again the next day.
q

My Teams chat and phone started blowing up! People were so relieved to hear they weren’t the only ones feeling this way. They thanked me for my honesty. It felt good to know I helped a few people on the team take a collective exhale. Show and tell got more honest for the rest of the week. It didn’t come back that next Monday.
h
2. Our jobs have wide salary ranges — how can we be up-front about that without every candidate expecting the top of the range?
q
Thank you to all the comments on the original post. As I looked through them, I saw many people with confusion regarding the different between “salary band” and “hiring range.” To clarify:
li

The salary band is the entire amount (no lower, no higher) that the HR team will allow to be paid for anyone within the role as the role is currently written and where it is currently based geographically. The band would change if the job duties were changed or if it was based in a different city/state.
li
The hiring range is the amount within the salary band that I as the hiring manager am budgeting for and planning to offer to the incoming candidate for the role based on their experience.
q
I live in a state where the entire salary band must legally be posted in its entirety, regardless of what the hiring range is.
q

I received many applicants who did not understand this, and even though they barely met the minimum requirements (or didn’t meet them at all), expected to be starting at $110,000. Unfortunately, my HR department didn’t update the listing as Alison suggested, so I had to push through my search with it as-is.
q

However, I am pleased to report that I have filled the position with someone with the exact amount of experience I was hoping for (not too junior but still room for growth), and was able to offer them just above the mid-point of the salary band. It appears that this salary was a nice step up from what they were making previously, and I am looking forward to working with them on expanding their role into something more (and, of course, increasing their salary band) over the next couple of years!
h
3. My boss is getting rid of everyone’s favorite part of my program for no good reason
q
Well, it worked out how I thought. I had to deal with many unhappy people. I said bouncy house for anonymity, but I’ll share that they were poultry we rehomed. I’m also the first letter in this link.
q

Many folks who visit our program and just people in the neighborhood were very sad, and occasionally irate to see the ducks were gone. I often said, “it was an administrative decision,” but occasionally I’d give out publicly available contact information to folks if I was feeling particularly ungenerous. I mostly got over it, but it certainly took a while and I maintain that the program is worse off.
q
The good news is I recently accepted a new position! It’s to a job with more authority, so hopefully I’ll be slightly less at the whims of others.
h
4. Including things from elementary school on a resume (#5 at the link)
q

I wrote last year for resume advice on behalf of my son, who was in college and had switched majors very recently, and needed to update his resume ASAP for leadership training program with a rapidly-approaching deadline. He followed your advice not to include some things his dad was pushing to include to “show he’s a good person” like elementary-school volunteering.
q

Some commenters were irate that we his parents were involved in his resume writing and made some interesting leaps about whether we were “helicopter parents.” They might or might not be pleased to find out that we collectively realized that his sister reads college student resumes as a major part of her job, so he ended up going to her for additional advice, and she helped him write a new and improved resume. (She also explained why he should never, ever use ChatGPT for his cover letter, and he listened. Hooray for siblings.)
q

While he didn’t get the position he was applying to when I wrote, he did get a job just after graduation in May and is really enjoying it. He makes more money than I do now. I answer his questions only when asked, and they are usually about cooking.
